newsitem.title: USA: U.S. thrifts could get EPS boost from legislation.
newsitem.headline: U.S. thrifts could get EPS boost from legislation.

text.p: Annual profits at U.S. thrifts could rise as much as 10 percent if a proposal to rescue the thrift deposit insurance fund is approved by Congress.
The legislation, caught in a web of industry disagreement during this and previous congressional sessions, has been gaining momentum, and some observers predict it will be adopted soon.
According to industry analysts, the plan could boost annual earnings at thrifts by about 10 percent.

Treasury Undersecretary John Hawke said on Friday that contentious issues in the regulatory relief portion of the legislation were worked out overnight and are now acceptable to the Clinton administration.
Provisions to bolster the Savings Association Insurance Fund (SAIF) were agreed on some time ago, but other provisions to ease regulatory burdens on banks needed to be ironed out.
"Our number one priority has always been getting BIF/SAIF done," Hawke told Reuters in Washington. "I think getting BIF/SAIF done now is a virtual certainty."
BIF refers to the Bank Insurance Fund (BIF), which insures deposits at banks. BIF/SAIF refers to the proposal to bolster the thrift deposit insurance fund.
Thrifts currently pay premiums of 23 basis points, or $0.23, per $100 of deposits. Banks pay no premiums due to a well capitalized BIF.
Banks had previously opposed the measure to bolster the undercapitalized SAIF because in earlier versions it would have cost them about $12 billion over 20 years.
"Due to certain revisions, the cost to banks has been somewhat reduced and opposition is softening," said Charlotte Birch, a spokeswoman for the American Bankers Association.
"This is not a bill that bankers will enthusiastically cheer, but it's a significant improvement over originally proposed BIF/SAIF legislation," she said.
The ultimate aim is to have banks and thrifts pay the same modest premiums.
Thrifts would have to pay an initial $4.7 billion to build up the SAIF, while banks would pick up part of the tab on bonds issued to pay for the previous savings and loan bailout.

"Clearly, there has been a tremendous amount of momentum on the SAIF/BIF front," said Lou Nevins, president of the Western League of Savings Institutions, a trade group for West Coast thrifts. "We have a basic package that both banks and thrifts are in agreement on."
Thrifts have faced several setbacks in the past, such as in April when the SAIF rescue plan was stripped from the federal budget.
Nevertheless, analysts and industry sources feel the legislation will eventually succeed.
Analysts says that once it goes through, most thrift analysts would revise upward their operating earnings estimates for thrifts because SAIF premiums would go down.

In a recent interview, Tad Lowrey, chief executive officer of Pasadena-based CENFED Bank, said that if the issue were resolved, CENFED's annual earnings could be boosted by $0.28 a share. CENFED reported 1995 profits of $1.57 a share.
